chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hasan al-Mithammi, from Muhammad al-Katib, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Amr, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Amr al-Azraq, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: A man asked him about a man who died and left behind a daughter of his brother, and left behind mawali (freedmen/patrons), and I had one thousand dirhams of his money with me, and no one knew about it. Then the daughter of his brother came and pledged a Mus'haf (copy of the Quran) with me, so I gave her thirty dirhams. Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me when I told him, 'Did anyone know about it?' I said, 'No.' He said, 'Then give it to her, piece by piece, and no one should know.'

key_terms.قِطْعَةً قِطْعَةً: Piece by piece (gradually or in installments)
key_terms.لَمْ يَعْلَمْ بِهَا أَحَدٌ: No one knew about it (exclusive knowledge)
key_terms.مَوَالِيَ: Mawali (freedmen or patrons, often considered heirs in Shia fiqh)

ai.seo_question: How is inheritance distributed when the deceased's estate is known only to one person and an heir pledges an item for a small debt?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the distribution of an estate when a single holder possesses knowledge of the debt, ruling that the heir (here, a paternal niece) is entitled to the full amount rather than it being split among multiple heirs. The scholar emphasizes the condition of exclusivity in knowledge ('la ya'lamu biha ahad'), ensuring that the heir receives the complete value without deduction for potential unknown co-heirs. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that the burden of proof for additional heirs lies with those who claim them, protecting the known heir's rights when the debt holder acts in good faith.
